title: The Secret of the Blinking Light
markdown:
In the emerald heart of Whispering Woods, Zara the naturalist and Wren the stoat were charting beetle flight — counts, directions, a sketch of a stag beetle that Wren insisted had winked — when a faint rhythmic blinking pulsed from the shadows. Blink. Blink-blink. Blink. Not a beetle. Not a coincidence they could file under wings. Zara’s scholar heart thrummed. “What is that?”

Wren twitched his nose. “A lost star playing hide-and-seek?”

They mimicked the pattern with leaves. The light pulsed on, persistent, urgent. A mystery that demanded understanding, not a matching game.

A voice, calm as moss on a stone, flowed through the trees. Ranger Suri, the woods’ steadfast guardian, gaze warm. “You’ve found its signal. This beacon speaks a simple language. Never truly ON, nor truly OFF for long. ON, or OFF. Two states. That is all.”

A dawning spark. Suri tapped a twig on a stone. Tap. Tap-tap. Tap. “Imagine this is your light. Tap is OFF, tap-tap is ON. The message is in the order.” Sequences. OFF, ON, OFF, ON. “Like the number one. ON, ON, OFF, OFF — like two.”

Wren’s whiskers twitched. “A code.”

Zara felt a thrill, a shiver of discovery. Binary. The language of ON and OFF.

Swift as an arrow they set to work. Confusion gone, buzzing in its place. Each ON a 1, each OFF a 0, pencils dancing across Zara’s sketchbook. The jumble looked like forest gibberish:

01100101 01101100 01100100 01100101 01110010 00100000 01100010 01100101 01100101 01100101 00100000 01110111 01100101 01110011 01110100 00100000 01101111 01100110 00100000 01110111 01101111 00100000 01110100 01110010 01100101 01100101

Suri’s smile was the last key. “Each group of eight is one letter.”

The gibberish became a sentence: Elder bee west of woe tree. Lost glow-worms, west of the Elder Bee tree, near thorny shadows.

Hearts pounding, they raced. Dawn painted rose and gold — a race against dimness. Following the directions they found the glow-worms huddled, tiny lights faint with fear, wings cool and papery. Zara’s hands guided them. Wren chirped, keeping little legs moving, a stoat traffic warden.

As the last glow-worm blinked, reunited, Zara breathed, “Binary. ON and OFF told us where to go.”

Suri nodded. She did not ask what else the language could unlock. Zara boxed the eight-bit groups in the sketchbook, marked the Elder Bee on her beetle map so nobody would call it a woe tree twice, and let Wren claim he had invented tap-tap. The woods, for a morning, spoke in two states, which was enough.
